title: INTEGRATING UNIVERSAL GENERATIVE AI PLATFORMS IN EDUCATIONAL LABS TO FOSTER CRITICAL THINKING AND DIGITAL LITERACY
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how general-purpose generative AI platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other text, image, and video generators can be integrated into instruction in ways that promote critical thinking and digital literacy rather than uncritical dependence on AI outputs. The authors are concerned that students may use GenAI to complete coursework superficially and may trust plausible but inaccurate responses. In response, they propose reframing AI limitations, especially hallucinations and inaccuracies, as opportunities for learning through structured critical evaluation.

The intervention is an interdisciplinary laboratory model in which students, after they have already learned course content, create prompts and test multiple GenAI systems on questions with known answers. Students then evaluate the accuracy, completeness, coherence, and quality of AI-generated text, images, and videos using a rubric and compare the performance of different tools. The paper describes a pilot implementation of this model in a general astronomy course, including text-based chatbot comparison, AI-generated astronomical imagery, and AI-generated video tasks.

The population consisted of undergraduate students in a general astronomy course for non-science majors at Borough of Manhattan Community College, part of CUNY, in New York, USA. The activity was implemented across several student cohorts over multiple semesters, with each lab session lasting two academic hours. Students worked in an educational lab/classroom context, and some extended their work outside class by posting projects to a course Facebook group or adapting them into symposium posters.

The main conclusions are that the AI-integrated lab generated high student engagement, initiative, peer discussion, creativity, and critical evaluation of AI outputs. The authors argue that text-based GenAI tools currently have the strongest immediate educational value, while image- and video-based tools are more suitable for creative exploratory tasks because of accuracy limitations. However, the study does not include a control group, standardized outcome measures, or long-term follow-up, so its conclusions are primarily pedagogical and exploratory rather than causal.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a descriptive pilot implementation with qualitative/observational evidence only. The paper explicitly notes the absence of a control group, standardized outcome measures, and reproducible experimental design, so it provides limited causal credibility.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests positive but unclear impact on engagement, critical thinking, and astronomy learning, with no effect sizes or comparative evidence. Impacts are promising but insufficiently quantified and not directly relevant to K-12 literacy outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Students in a general astronomy lab use general-purpose LLM chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Copilot to generate answers to astronomy questions they already know, then critically compare and evaluate response accuracy, completeness, and reasoning.

Students use generative image and video AI tools to create speculative astronomical images and short videos as multimodal exploratory lab tasks supporting creativity and discussion, though these are not evaluated as rigorously as the text-based chatbots.

finding.finding_summary: Across several cohorts in a college general astronomy course, the authors report high student engagement, initiative, and intrinsic motivation during and after the AI-integrated lab. Evidence is descriptive only: students voluntarily continued projects outside class, shared products in a course Facebook group, and some adapted work into symposium posters, but no standardized engagement instrument, control group, or effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Observed engagement, voluntary continuation of work, participation in online sharing and symposium presentations

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that students developed critical evaluation skills, better prompt design, and more reflective use of AI by distinguishing fully correct, partially correct, and incorrect outputs using a rubric. Findings are based on instructor observation and narrative description rather than validated pre/post assessment; no sample size or quantitative effect estimates are provided.
finding.measure: Observed critical thinking, prompt engineering, evaluative judgment of AI outputs using rubric categories

finding.finding_summary: The authors claim the lab deepened students' comprehension of astronomy content by requiring them to generate domain-relevant questions, compare AI answers against known course knowledge, and discuss inaccuracies. However, there was no control group, no standardized science assessment, and no reported learning gains, so the positive finding is suggestive and based on descriptive classroom evidence only.
finding.measure: Course-embedded astronomy question design, accuracy checking of AI responses, class discussion of scientific content
